ref: Leg. 10 (chapter per Bull, Bethune-Baker n.2 and Dorner n.1); Bull Book II ch. IV sec. 9 (Parker 1851 numbering)
greek: ἀλλ᾽ ἔστιν ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ λόγος τοῦ πατρὸς ἐν ἰδέᾳ καὶ ἐνεργείᾳ. πρὸς αὐτοῦ γὰρ καὶ δι᾽ αὐτοῦ πάντα ἐγένετο, ἑνὸς ὄντος τοῦ πατρὸς καὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ· ὄντος δὲ τοῦ υἱοῦ ἐν πατρί, καὶ πατρὸς ἐν υἱῷ, ἑνότητι καὶ δυνάμει πνεύματος, νοῦς καὶ λόγος τοῦ πατρὸς ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ.
greek_edition: Greek as printed in Bull's footnote c (p.152) of the Parker 1851 English translation, read from the archive.org scan text layer (OCR). OCR read 'ὃ vids' and was corrected to ὁ υἱὸς; the rest is as printed. Not checked against Otto or Schwartz.
english: But the Son of God is the Word of the Father, in idea and in operation. For by Him and through Him were all things made, the Father and the Son being One; and, the Son being in the Father, and the Father in the Son, by the unity and power of the Spirit: the Son of God is the mind and Word of God. (Bull's own English rendering, as printed)
translator: Not named in the scan (Parker 1851 'A New Translation'; the translator is not identified in the text read)
edition: George Bull, Defensio Fidei Nicaenae ('A New Translation', Oxford: John Henry Parker, 1851)
what_it_says: Bull reads Leg. 10 as stating that the Son is one with the Father in essence and power, and that no Arian could have said it.
limits: This is Bull's 17th-century apologetic reading, not Athenagoras's own vocabulary (no homoousios in the text). Bull takes 'πρὸς αὐτοῦ' as 'by Him'; a Benedictine editor cited by Bull dislikes that reading (note h, p.153, PDF p.177), and ANF/Pratten renders it 'after the pattern of Him and by Him'.

ref: Leg. 10 (Bull's citation of 'p.10 ad calcem Just. Mart.' Paris 1615); Bull Book II ch. IV sec. 9
greek_edition: Bull's Greek fragment only (footnote-quoted in Bull p.153, PDF p.177); the full Greek sentence is not reproduced in the scan. Read from OCR text layer.
english: Presently after, however, in the same passage, Athenagoras distinctly denies, that the Son in the beginning came forth from the Father to create all things 'as made,' (ὡς γενόμενον) or created by God, [a denial] which aims a deadly blow at the Arian blasphemy.
edition: George Bull, Defensio Fidei Nicaenae ('A New Translation', Oxford: John Henry Parker, 1851)
what_it_says: Bull reads Athenagoras as denying that the Son was created 'as made', which Bull takes as anti-Arian.
limits: Bull's gloss. Newman, Bethune-Baker and Dorner read the same denial as a denial of 'coming into being', not as a full Nicene statement. The Greek sentence itself was not read in this pass.

ref: Leg. 10 (Bull's citation); Bull Book II ch. IV sec. 9
greek: καὶ ἀπόρροια, ὡς φῶς ἀπὸ πυρὸς, τὸ πνεῦμα
greek_edition: Greek as printed in Bull's footnote i (p.153, PDF p.177) of the Parker 1851 translation; read from OCR text layer; not checked against Otto or Schwartz.
english: ...the Holy Ghost also flows forth and emanates from God the Father Himself, (through the Son, that is to say, as we have shewn above,) as light proceeds from fire. In passing you may observe, how completely Athenagoras acknowledged the consubstantiality of the Holy Ghost, equally with that of the Son. (Bull p.154, PDF p.178)
edition: George Bull, Defensio Fidei Nicaenae ('A New Translation', Oxford: John Henry Parker, 1851)
what_it_says: Bull reads Athenagoras's 'effluence like light from fire' as the Spirit's emanation from the Father and as the consubstantiality of the Spirit.
limits: Bull's reading. The word 'consubstantiality' is Bull's, not Athenagoras's. Loofs (A9-21) denies that the Spirit's personhood is clear in Athenagoras.

ref: Leg. 10 (Bull's citation, Justin appendix Paris 1615); Bull Book I, Athenagoras sec. 10
greek: ἀλλὰ τοῦτο τὸ τῷ ὄντι ἀπὸ τοῦ Πατρὸς προβληθὲν γέννημα πρὸ πάντων τῶν ποιημάτων συνῆν τῷ Πατρὶ, καὶ
greek_edition: Greek fragment as printed in Bull's footnote (p.53, PDF p.77); OCR; not checked against Otto or Schwartz.
english: He also, a little after, calls the Son 'the first offspring of the Father, as having come forth [from Him] to be the idea and energy of all things.' (Bull p.53, PDF p.77)
edition: George Bull, Defensio Fidei Nicaenae ('A New Translation', Oxford: John Henry Parker, 1851)
what_it_says: Bull paraphrases Athenagoras's 'first offspring' as having come forth to be idea and energy of all things, while already with the Father before creation.
limits: Bull's paraphrase with his own bracket '[from Him]'. Athenagoras's Greek is only fragmentary here.

ref: Leg. 10 (Newman cites Bull, Defens. iii.5 sec.2 for the Greek); Newman ch. XI sec. III
greek: ἰδέα καὶ ἐνέργεια (fragment in Newman's footnote, OCR-garbled)
greek_edition: Newman gives Greek only in fragments in footnotes (p.170), citing Bull Defens. iii.5 sec.2; OCR-garbled, not used as exact Greek.
english: ...the first-born of the Father; not as made, for God being Mind Eternal, had from the beginning reason in Himself, being eternally intellectual; but as issuing forth upon the chaotic mass as the Idea and Agent of Creation.
translator: Not named in the text; Newman's own rendering (unattributed)
edition: John Henry Cardinal Newman, The Arians of the Fourth Century, 7th ed., London: Longmans, Green & Co., 1890
what_it_says: Newman states that Athenagoras makes the Son eternal in the Father, with the 'going-forth' only for creation.
limits: Newman's English, not a named translation; 'first-born' for πρῶτον γέννημα (ANF/Pratten: 'first product'). Newman uses this to argue for the Logos eternity, not for the Nicene formula.

ref: Leg. 10 (Newman p.172 cites 'the passage lately referred to'; Newman ch. XI sec. III)
greek_edition: No Greek in Newman's text for this passage (English only, OCR text layer).
english: Thus Athenagoras, in the passage lately referred to, says; 'Let no one ridicule the notion that God has a Son. ... But the Son of God is the Word of the Father [as Creator] both in idea and in active power' ... the Father and the Son being one. The Son being in the Father, and the Father in the Son, in the unity and power of the Spirit, the Son of God is the Mind and Word of the Father.
translator: Not named; Newman's rendering (unattributed); bracket '[as Creator]' is Newman's
edition: John Henry Cardinal Newman, The Arians of the Fourth Century, 7th ed., London: Longmans, Green & Co., 1890
what_it_says: Newman presents Athenagoras's 'Son in the Father, Father in the Son, by unity and power of the Spirit' as a Nicene-type statement of coinherence.
limits: Newman's English with his own insertion; he does not show the Spirit as a distinct person here.

ref: Leg. 10 (metaphor of 'Logos' in Newman's general discussion, ch. XI sec. III)
greek_edition: English only (OCR text layer).
english: Its obvious tendency was to obliterate the notion of the Son's Personality, that is, to introduce Sabellianism. ... And it was to counteract this tendency, that is, to witness against it, that the Fathers speak of Him as the Word in an hypostasis, the permanent, real, and living Word.
edition: John Henry Cardinal Newman, The Arians of the Fourth Century, 7th ed., London: Longmans, Green & Co., 1890
what_it_says: Newman says the 'going-forth' metaphor, if pressed, tended toward Sabellianism, which the Fathers countered with 'hypostasis'.
limits: About the metaphor in general (Origen, Athenagoras and others), not Athenagoras alone. Newman reads the Fathers' answer as hypostasis, which is his own reading.

ref: Leg. 10 (charge discussed by Newman, ch. XI sec. III)
greek_edition: English only (OCR text layer).
english: The Fathers, who have laid themselves open to this charge, are Athenagoras, Tatian, Theophilus, Hippolytus, and Novatian, as mentioned in the first Chapter. Now that they did not mean what a superficial reader might lay to their charge, may be argued, first, from the parallel language of the Post-Nicenes, ...
edition: John Henry Cardinal Newman, The Arians of the Fourth Century, 7th ed., London: Longmans, Green & Co., 1890
what_it_says: Newman admits that Athenagoras and others 'laid themselves open' to the charge that the Son began to exist in a second person, and then defends them by the Post-Nicene language.
limits: Newman's concession and defence, not a quotation of Athenagoras. Newman's defence continues beyond the line read here; not read in full.

ref: Leg. 10 (Bethune-Baker sec. 'Athenagoras: his fuller recognition'); index entry 'Athenagoras, doctrine of the Logos, 128'
greek_edition: English only; Bethune-Baker quotes Athenagoras in English.
english: In Athenagoras is found a clearer view of the personal existence of the Logos (or the Son) before Creation, and a fuller perception of the problem how to secure the unity and yet assign its due place to the distinction.
edition: J. F. Bethune-Baker, An Introduction to the Early History of Christian Doctrine, London: Methuen, 1903
what_it_says: Bethune-Baker says Athenagoras presents the Logos as personally existing before creation, a point he sees as a link to later formulations.
limits: Bethune-Baker's view; he also says 'the distinctions in the being of God are thus conceived as self-existent', which opponents will read as subordinationist.

ref: Scholarship on Athenagoras's Logos (Loofs as quoted by Bethune-Baker, n. and text, p.128)
greek_edition: English only.
english: ...it is not God who reveals Himself in Christ, but the Logos, the depotentiated God, a God who as God is subordinate to the highest God (Loofs).
translator: Quoted in English by Bethune-Baker (translator of Loofs's German not named)
edition: J. F. Bethune-Baker, An Introduction to the Early History of Christian Doctrine, London: Methuen, 1903
what_it_says: Loofs's subordinationist criticism of the Apologists' Logos, quoted by Bethune-Baker.
limits: Loofs's criticism quoted second-hand by Bethune-Baker; the German original was read separately (A9-19 to A9-21). Bethune-Baker says the criticism's limits have been noted.

ref: Leg. 10 (Bethune-Baker cites 'Leg. 10' in n.2 at p.129); Leg. 12 for 'παῖς' (n.1 p.129)
greek_edition: English; Bethune-Baker names the best edition as E. Schwartz, Leipzig 1891 (TU iv 2), and says the Son is called παῖς in Leg. 12 (OCR 'TTCUS').
english: ...'not as having come into being (for from the beginning God, since He is eternal Mind, had in Himself the Logos (reason), since He is eternally possessed of Logos (rational)); but as having proceeded forth as idea and energy (i.e. in exercise of the idea)'. 'God's Son is the Logos of the Father in idea and in operation.' He has thus a previous relation to the Father, as has the Holy Spirit ...
edition: J. F. Bethune-Baker, An Introduction to the Early History of Christian Doctrine, London: Methuen, 1903
what_it_says: Bethune-Baker reads Athenagoras's 'first begotten' as personal and pre-creation, and says the three names mark eternally existing distinctions within God.
limits: Bethune-Baker's view that the three names are 'eternally existing distinctions' is his interpretation. The Schwartz 1891 edition is named but not checked here.

ref: Leg. 10 (effluence passage, per Bethune-Baker and Loofs n.2)
greek_edition: English only.
english: ...Athenagoras, who sees in the Spirit the bond of union by which the Father and Son coinhere, and implies the doctrine of his essential procession by the image in which he describes him as an effluence from God, emanating from Him and returning to Him as a ray of the sun or as light from fire.
edition: J. F. Bethune-Baker, An Introduction to the Early History of Christian Doctrine, London: Methuen, 1903
what_it_says: Bethune-Baker reads the 'effluence' image as implying the Spirit's essential procession and as the bond of the Father and Son.
limits: 'Implies' is Bethune-Baker's inference; the scan does not show him stating the Spirit is a distinct person in Athenagoras.

ref: Leg. 9 (Bethune-Baker n.2 at p.46 cites 'Legatio 9')
greek_edition: English only.
english: In Athenagoras ... we find a description of the process of inspiration derived from purely pagan sources. The Spirit uses men as its instruments, playing upon them as a flute-player blows a flute.
edition: J. F. Bethune-Baker, An Introduction to the Early History of Christian Doctrine, London: Methuen, 1903
what_it_says: Bethune-Baker reads Athenagoras's inspiration as mechanical and pagan-derived, the Spirit as an instrument.
limits: Bethune-Baker's characterisation. Athenagoras's sentence (ANF/Pratten, Leg. 9) also says the prophets were 'lifted in ecstasy'; this is the mantic-instrument reading that opponents use against personhood.

ref: Leg. 10 (Dorner p.283 cites 'Leg. 10' and 'Leg. 12'); Dorner Div. I sec. 'Athenagoras'
greek_edition: English only.
english: The representation of the hypostatizing of the Logos at the creation is rejected utterly by the clearer and more cautious Athenagoras, who, through his purer concept of God, opens a way to an immanent relation between the Father and Son.
edition: I. A. Dorner, History of the Development of the Doctrine of the Person of Christ, Div. I, vol. I, transl. W. L. Alexander, Edinburgh: T. & T. Clark, 1861
what_it_says: Dorner says Athenagoras rejects making the Logos a separate hypostasis at creation and opens an immanent relation of Father and Son.
limits: Dorner's 'immanent relation' is his own category (his 'development' scheme), not Nicene; he also doubts Athenagoras's Logos is immanent in God (A9-15).

ref: Leg. 10 (Dorner n.1 on p.284: 'Leg. 10: ...ἐν ἰδέᾳ καὶ ἐνεργείᾳ'); Dorner Div. I sec. 'Athenagoras'
greek: ἐστι ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ λόγος τοῦ πατρὸς ἐν ἰδέᾳ καὶ ἐνεργείᾳ
greek_edition: Dorner's footnote 1 on p.284 (PDF p.308); OCR reads 'tori 6 vids rod Ozod Adyos tov warpdc ev idéee noel Evepryeiee'; 'ἐστι' is inferred from OCR 'tori'. Not checked against Otto or Schwartz.
english: Athenagoras does not regard the Logos as first begotten at the creation of the world ... God's Son, the knowledge of whom the Christians have, is the Logos of the Father in idea and in operation; ... Athenagoras will not allow the being of the Son to be expended merely in relation to the world; he ascribes to Him a previous relation to the Father.
edition: I. A. Dorner, History of the Development of the Doctrine of the Person of Christ, Div. I, vol. I, transl. W. L. Alexander, Edinburgh: T. & T. Clark, 1861
what_it_says: Dorner argues Athenagoras's Son has a being prior to and apart from the world-idea, so the creation is not the source of the Son's being.
limits: Dorner also says it 'may be doubted' whether the Logos is the idea of the world at all, and that the Son's essence could be 'simply to be the idea of the world' (p.284); not a full answer to the 'created Logos' charge.

ref: Leg. 10, 12 (Dorner p.283 on names; Dorner cites Leg. 16 and de Resurr. 12 for the wider argument)
greek_edition: English only.
english: For the rest, the doctrine of the Holy Ghost is the central-point of his system rather than that of Jesus or Christ, neither of which names occurs in his Apology (Cohort. ad Graec.).
edition: I. A. Dorner, History of the Development of the Doctrine of the Person of Christ, Div. I, vol. I, transl. W. L. Alexander, Edinburgh: T. & T. Clark, 1861
what_it_says: Dorner says 'Jesus' and 'Christ' do not occur in the Plea and the Holy Spirit is the centre of Athenagoras's thought.
limits: Dorner's claim. Checked in ANF/Pratten English (Plea and De resurrectione): no 'Jesus', no whole-word 'Christ', no 'Trinity' or 'Triad'; the Greek word count was not checked (negative result is English only).

ref: Dorner Notes, n. on Theophilus and Athenagoras (Spirit = divine essence); ref Leg. 12 'unity and power of the Spirit'
greek_edition: English only.
english: Athenagoras says,—Father and Son interpenetrate each other, in virtue of the unity and power of their spirit:—by Spirit must, in this case again, be understood the common Divine essence.
edition: I. A. Dorner, History of the Development of the Doctrine of the Person of Christ, Div. I, vol. I, transl. W. L. Alexander, Edinburgh: T. & T. Clark, 1861
what_it_says: Dorner reads 'the unity and power of the Spirit' in Athenagoras as the common divine essence, not the Holy Spirit as a third person.
limits: This is Dorner's reading and it is contested by Trinitarian readers; Bull (A9-03) reads the Spirit as consubstantial. Genuine ambiguity in the Greek: the Spirit can be read either way.

ref: Harnack, History of Dogma vol. I, ch. on the Apologists / Neoplatonism context
greek_edition: English only.
english: The earliest Christian philosophers, especially Justin and Athenagoras, likewise prepared the way for the speculations of the later Neoplatonists by their attempts, on the one hand, to connect Christianity with Stoicism and Platonism, and on the other, to exhibit it as supra-Platonic.
translator: Neil Buchanan (Theological Translation Library, 1897 printing per scan)
edition: Adolf Harnack, History of Dogma, vol. I, transl. Neil Buchanan, Theological Translation Library, Williams & Norgate (1897 printing per scan)
what_it_says: Harnack places Athenagoras among the philosophical apologists who paved the way for Neoplatonic speculation about God.
limits: General remark, not about the Trinity; Harnack's own view of the Logos is not read here. Included as context for the 'Hellenisation' objection.

ref: Loofs §18 (3)(c), German text; Leg. 12 cited (supplic. 12 p.54-55 Otto), Leg. 10 (supplic. 10 p.48)
greek_edition: German text read from archive.org djvu OCR; Loofs's Greek is printed in a Latin-letter encoding and is not reproduced here. PDF page capture not possible (PDF 90 MB > 60 MB limit).
english: Own translation: Athenagoras explains the 'first begotten' (πρῶτον γέννημα) of the Father by 'not as having come into being' ... and all these expressions express the same thought: the begottenness of the Logos is distinguished from creation.
edition: Friedrich Loofs, Leitfaden zum Studium der Dogmengeschichte, 4th ed., Halle a.S.: Max Niemeyer, 1906
what_it_says: Loofs says Athenagoras uses 'first begotten', 'not as made' to distinguish the Son's begottenness from the creation.
limits: Loofs also says the Apologists' Logos is not yet a clear personal God (A9-21). Greek encoding is unreliable in the OCR.

ref: Loofs §18 (3)(c), German; Leg. 12 (supplic. 12) and Leg. 10 cited in n.
greek_edition: German text from djvu OCR; no Greek reproduced.
english: Own translation: Athenagoras emphasises the unity of the Son and the Father.
edition: Friedrich Loofs, Leitfaden zum Studium der Dogmengeschichte, 4th ed., Halle a.S.: Max Niemeyer, 1906
what_it_says: Loofs notes that Athenagoras stresses the unity of Son and Father, but says the concept of God's personality was not yet sharply grasped, so the unity of the divine substance is emphasised.
limits: Loofs's point that personality was not yet sharply grasped cuts against a Nicene reading.

ref: Loofs §18 (5a), German, footnote 2 on p.126 (Leg. 10, supplic. 10 p.48; Leg. 24 p.124 per Loofs)
greek_edition: German text from djvu OCR; the Greek fragment in the footnote is in Loofs's Latin-letter encoding and not reproduced.
english: Own translation: Athenagoras, who calls the Spirit an 'apóppoia' of God, also clearly distinguishes it from the Logos ... The personality of the Spirit is therefore as uncertain as that of many powers.
edition: Friedrich Loofs, Leitfaden zum Studium der Dogmengeschichte, 4th ed., Halle a.S.: Max Niemeyer, 1906
what_it_says: Loofs says the personhood of the Spirit in Athenagoras is uncertain, comparable to many powers.
limits: Loofs's assessment; he also says the Spirit is clearly distinguished from the Logos (body text, p.126). Contrasts with Bull and Bethune-Baker (A9-03, A9-12).

ref: Loofs §18 (5a), German, p.126; Theophilus (ad Autol. II.15) and Leg. 12 cited
greek_edition: German text from djvu OCR; Greek not reproduced.
english: Own translation: Although the triadic formulas that resemble the baptismal formula are found among the Apologists, they are not to be understood as formulas of a doctrine of Trinity of the Apologists. They are rather a sign of the pagan-philosophical elasticity of their monotheism.
edition: Friedrich Loofs, Leitfaden zum Studium der Dogmengeschichte, 4th ed., Halle a.S.: Max Niemeyer, 1906
what_it_says: Loofs says the Apologists' triad-type formulas are not a doctrine of the Trinity but a sign of an elastic monotheism.
limits: Loofs's position. Trinitarian readers reply that the 'power in unity and distinction in order' (Leg. 10, Pratten) is structured, not merely a list.

ref: Leg. 10 (Pratten/ANF English; chapter division per Bethune-Baker and Loofs)
greek_edition: English primary text read from newadvent (ANF); the Greek was not checked in this pass.
english: Proverbs 8:22 The Holy Spirit Himself also, which operates in the prophets, we assert to be an effluence of God, flowing from Him, and returning back again like a beam of the sun.
edition: B. P. Pratten, ANF vol. 2 (newadvent.org/fathers/0205.htm), Ante-Nicene Fathers, public domain
what_it_says: Athenagoras calls the Holy Spirit an effluence of God, flowing from Him and returning like a sun-ray.
limits: The effluence image itself does not settle personhood; Loofs (A9-21) and Dorner (A9-17) read it as a power or the divine essence.

ref: Leg. 10 (Pratten/ANF English; chapter per Dorner n.1 and Bethune-Baker n.2)
greek_edition: English primary text read from newadvent (ANF); Greek not checked in this pass.
english: But if, in your surpassing intelligence, it occurs to you to inquire what is meant by the Son, I will state briefly that He is the first product of the Father, not as having been brought into existence (for from the beginning, God, who is the eternal mind [νοῦς], had the Logos in Himself, being from eternity instinct with Logos [λογικός]); but inasmuch as He came forth to be the idea and energizing power of all material things, ...
edition: B. P. Pratten, ANF vol. 2 (newadvent.org/fathers/0205.htm), Ante-Nicene Fathers, public domain
what_it_says: Athenagoras says the Son is the first product of the Father, not as brought into existence, since God had the Logos in Himself from eternity, but as coming forth for creation.
limits: This is the core hard passage (Leg. 10). The 'came forth' clause supports the endiathetic/prophorikos reading that Newman and Dorner discuss; the Greek was not verified here.
